title: Experience and change
cando: connect the past to now, and describe how things have changed

about.text: In this lesson you connect the past to now. You talk about how a job has changed, how long you have been doing something, and what you have learned. You read about a furniture maker's twenty years at the same bench, and you tell an old friend how your life has changed.
goals: Say how long you have been doing something: I've been working here for ten years.
Choose the past simple or the present perfect: I started in 2015. I've worked here since 2015.
Describe how a job or a town has changed.
Read an article and a training record, and write about what has changed.
Tell a friend what has happened and what you have learned.

chapters.title: How the job changed
chapters.text:
This lesson is about change: in your job, in your town, and in you.
First, you listen to Mei and Omar. They work at a parcel depot. Mei has just started, and Omar has been there for more than fifteen years.
Omar says: Things have changed a lot since I started. In those days, we sorted every parcel by hand. Now there are automatic machines, and everything is digital.
Listen for how Omar felt about the change, and what he has been doing since his promotion.

chapters.title: Past simple, present perfect, and I've been working
chapters.text:
Now, the grammar. English has two main ways to talk about the past, and they say different things.
The past simple is for a finished time. I started here in 2010. They installed the machines last year.
The present perfect connects the past to now. I've worked here for ten years. That means: I still work here.
So when you say a finished time, like in 2010 or last year, use the past simple.
Then there is the present perfect continuous: have been, and the -ing form of the verb. It's for an activity that started in the past and is still going on. I've been working here since March. How long have you been learning English?
A very common mistake is: I am working here since March. Say: I've been working here since March.

chapters.title: Twenty years at the same bench
chapters.text:
Next, you read an article by Samir, a furniture maker. He has worked at the same bench for twenty years, and almost everything about his job has changed.
Then you read his training record. It shows the courses he has done this year, and how many hours he still needs. Read the numbers carefully.
After that, you write about what has changed in your own job, your studies or your town. Say what it was like when you started, and what it's like now.

chapters.title: Catching up with an old friend
chapters.text:
Then you meet an old friend in a café. You haven't seen each other for ten years. Your friend asks: What have you been doing? How has the town changed?
Tell your story in order. Say what you did before, in the past simple. Say what has changed, in the present perfect. And say how long you have been doing your job now.
Finish with one thing you have learned. For example: What I've learned is that change is hard at first, but it gets easier.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text: Last, you read a longer story or article about change. Read it once for the main idea: what changed, and how did people feel about it? Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: Think about your job, or a job you know well. What has changed most in the last ten years?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. In most jobs, many things change at once. In this lesson, you talk about how things have changed and what you have learned.

conversation.title: Fifteen years at the depot
conversation.setting: Mei has just started work at a parcel depot. At break time, she chats to Omar, who has worked there for a long time.
lines: How long have you worked here, Omar?
Since 2009. So I've been doing this for over fifteen years now.
Wow. Has the job changed much?
Things have changed a lot since I started. In those days, we sorted every parcel by hand.
Every single one. Then in 2015, they installed the automatic machines, and everything became digital.
At first, yes. My old routine was suddenly out of date, and I had to learn a new system. But I adapted gradually.
And now we rely on the scanners for everything.
Exactly. They update the software every few months, so you have to keep up to date.
Have you always worked on the day team?
No. I got a promotion three years ago, and I've been running the night team since then.
Did that come with a pay rise?
It did, a small one! But honestly, I've learned more in the last three years than in all the years before.

questions.q: How did the workers sort parcels when Omar started?
questions.why: Omar says: In those days, we sorted every parcel by hand.

questions.q: When did the depot install the automatic machines?
questions.why: Omar says: Then in 2015, they installed the automatic machines.

questions.q: What has Omar been doing since his promotion?
questions.why: He says: I've been running the night team since then.

items.meaning: To change the way you do things because the situation is different.
items.example: It took me a few months to adapt to working nights.

items.meaning: To put a machine or a computer program in place, ready to use.
items.example: The company installed new cameras in the car park.

items.meaning: To add the newest information or changes to something.
items.example: Please update your phone number on the system.

items.meaning: Working by itself, with no person controlling it.
items.example: The doors are automatic: they open when you walk towards them.

items.meaning: Using computers and electronic information, not paper.
items.example: All our records are digital now, so we hardly print anything.

items.meaning: The things you usually do, in the same order, every day.
items.example: My morning routine starts with coffee and my emails.

items.meaning: Happening or existing now.
items.example: Please write your current address on the form.

items.meaning: Happening or existing before this one.
items.example: In my previous job, I worked in a hotel.

items.meaning: A move to a more important job in the same company.
items.example: She got a promotion after only two years.

items.meaning: An increase in the money you get for your work.
items.example: Everyone in the team got a small pay rise in April.

items.meaning: To need someone or something, and trust them to help you or to work well.
items.example: We rely on the van drivers to get the parcels out on time.

items.meaning: Modern, or with the newest information.
items.example: Make sure your contact details are up to date.

items.meaning: Old, and not correct or useful any more.
items.example: This map is out of date: the new road isn't on it.

items.meaning: Slowly, in small steps, over a period of time.
items.example: Gradually, the new system became easier to use.

items.meaning: Done by a person, not by a machine.
items.example: We used to write every order by hand.

sound.title: I've been, she's been
sound.explain: In the present perfect continuous, the small words are quick and quiet. I've been sounds like ive-bin, and she's been sounds like sheez-bin. The main verb is strong: I've been WORKing here for ten years. Listen, then say each group. Keep the small words short.
groups: I've been · you've been · we've been
she's been · he's been · it's been
lines: I've been working here for ten years.
She's been waiting since nine o'clock.
How long have you been doing this job?

sayIt.instructions: Say Omar's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Are I've and been short and quiet?
lines: Since 2009. So I've been doing this for over fifteen years now.
Things have changed a lot since I started. In those days, we sorted every parcel by hand.
At first, yes. My old routine was suddenly out of date, and I had to learn a new system. But I adapted gradually.
No. I got a promotion three years ago, and I've been running the night team since then.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. They all talk about the past, but in different ways.
examples: I got a promotion three years ago.
Things have changed a lot since I started.
I've been running the night team since then.
spot.question: Which sentence gives a finished time? Which one connects the past to now? Which one is about an activity that is still going on?
spot.answer: I got a promotion three years ago is the past simple: three years ago is a finished time. Things have changed is the present perfect: from the past up to now. I've been running is the present perfect continuous: Omar started in the past, and he is still doing it.

rules.title: Past simple or present perfect?
rule: Past simple: a finished time. I started here in 2010. I left my last job two years ago.
Present perfect: from the past up to now. I've worked here for ten years. (I still work here.)
The present perfect often goes with since and for: since 2010, since I started, for ten years.
Ask When did you start? for a finished time, and How long have you worked here? for up to now.
rules.mistake: A finished time needs the past simple. Not: I have started this job in 2010. Say: I started this job in 2010.

rules.title: The present perfect continuous: I've been working
rule: have or has + been + -ing: I've been working here since March.
Use it for an activity that started in the past and is still going on: She's been waiting for an hour.
Ask with How long…? How long have you been learning English?
For a number of finished things, use the present perfect simple: I've written three reports today.
Some verbs don't take -ing: know, like, own, believe. I've known her for years.
rules.mistake: Not: I am working here since March. Say: I've been working here since March.

practice.why: 2012 is a finished time, so we use the past simple.
since + a point in the past, up to now: the present perfect.

practice.q: How long ___ you been learning English?
practice.why: The present perfect continuous: have + been + -ing.

practice.q: Where's the bus? We ___ for forty minutes!
practice.why: The waiting started in the past and is still going on.

practice.q: I ___ three reports so far today.
practice.why: A number of finished things: the present perfect simple.

practice.q: Your hands are dirty! What have you been ___ ?
practice.why: have been + the -ing form: What have you been doing?
When asks about a finished time, so we use the past simple.

practice.q: I ___ him for years. We went to school together.
practice.why: know doesn't take -ing: I've known him for years.

practice.q: Things ___ a lot since I started here.
practice.why: since I started = from the past up to now, so the present perfect.

practice.q: Last year the company ___ new machines.
practice.why: Last year is a finished time: the past simple.

yourTurn.prompt: Think about your job, your studies or your town. Write four or five sentences about how things have changed. Use the past simple for a finished time, the present perfect for up to now, and the present perfect continuous to say how long.
starters: Things have changed a lot since …
yourTurn.model: I started working at the hotel in 2016. In those days, we wrote every booking by hand. Things have changed a lot since then, and now everything is digital. I've been working on the front desk for four years, and I've learned a lot about people. Last year I got a promotion, so now I train new staff.

text.title: Twenty years at the same bench, and a training record
text.body:
TWENTY YEARS AT THE SAME BENCH
by Samir Haddad, furniture maker
I have worked at the same bench for twenty years, but almost nothing about the job is the same. When I started, we took every measurement by hand and wrote it on a card. Now the measurements come from a computer.
I qualified in 2006, and at the time I thought I had finished learning. I was wrong. The job has changed three times since then, and each time I have had to adapt. The first change was hard to accept. The second was easier.
The new machines are more accurate than I ever was, and that is fine. But a machine can't choose the right piece of wood. That still takes a skilled person and years of practice.
There are fewer of us in the trade now. When I started, forty people worked in this workshop. Today there are eleven. I have been teaching the younger staff for five years, and I still learn a new technique every year. The day I stop learning, I will retire.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE FORM: this association does not exist.
NORTHERN FURNITURE MAKERS' ASSOCIATION
Annual training record: 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026
Member: Samir Haddad   Membership number: 41-2288
Training so far: 24 of the compulsory 30 hours
Machine safety (refresher): 6 hours, completed
Computer design, part 1: 12 hours, completed
New finishing techniques: 6 hours, completed
Computer design, part 2: 6 hours, booked for 14 March
Has your work changed this year? Yes. I no longer cut every piece by hand. I now use a computer-controlled saw.
Members who do not complete 30 hours by 31 March lose their Registered Maker certificate. They get it back when they finish the missing hours.

gist.q: What is the article mainly about?
gist.a: how one man's job has changed over twenty years
wrong: how to become a furniture maker
why Samir wants to leave his job
gist.why: Samir describes how his work has changed since he started, twenty years ago.

gist.q: What does the training record show?
gist.a: the training a member has done this year
wrong: the hours Samir works every week
gist.why: It lists Samir's courses and his training hours so far this year.

detail.q: How did Samir take measurements when he started?
detail.why: He writes: When I started, we took every measurement by hand.

detail.q: How many people work in the workshop today?
detail.why: When I started, forty people worked in this workshop. Today there are eleven.

detail.q: How many more hours of training does Samir need before 31 March?
detail.why: He has done 24 of the 30 compulsory hours, and 30 − 24 = 6.

detail.q: What happens to members who don't complete 30 hours?
detail.a: They lose their certificate until they finish the hours.
wrong: They have to pay a fine.
detail.why: They lose their Registered Maker certificate, and get it back when they finish the missing hours.

items.meaning: To pass the exams or the training that you need for a job.
items.example: She qualified as a nurse in 2015.

items.meaning: A job that needs special skills with your hands, like plumbing or electrical work.
items.example: My father taught me the trade when I was sixteen.

items.meaning: Having the training and experience to do a job well.
items.example: We need two skilled workers for the new project.

items.meaning: A number that shows the size, length or amount of something.
items.example: Write down the measurements of the window before you order the glass.

items.meaning: Correct in every detail.
items.example: The new scales are more accurate than the old ones.

items.meaning: A particular way of doing something that needs skill.
items.example: He showed me a better technique for cutting glass.

items.meaning: An official paper that shows you have passed a course or an exam.
items.example: You'll get a certificate at the end of the course.

items.meaning: Happening once a year.
items.example: Our annual safety training is in March.

items.meaning: Being a member of a group or an organisation, often by paying money.
items.example: My gym membership costs thirty pounds a month.

items.meaning: Something you must do, because a rule says so.
items.example: Safety training is compulsory for all new staff.

items.meaning: Not now, although it was true before.
items.example: We no longer print the orders. Everything is on the screen.

model.title: What has changed in my job
model.body:
I've been working at the Greenway Hotel for twelve years. When I started, we kept all the bookings in a big book at the front desk, and we wrote every bill by hand. In 2018 the hotel installed a new computer system, and everything became digital. At first I found it difficult, but I adapted gradually.
Since then, the job has changed in other ways too. Most guests book online, so we no longer answer the phone all day. I've learned to use three different programs, and last year I got a promotion to front desk manager. The one thing that hasn't changed is the guests: they still want a friendly face when they arrive.

write.task: Write about what has changed in your job, your studies or your town. Write two paragraphs of 100–150 words: what it was like when you started, and what it is like now.
write.starter: I've been … for … years. When I started, …
checklist: I used the past simple for a finished time: In 2018, the hotel installed …
I used the present perfect for up to now: Since then, the job has changed …
I said how long with for or since: I've been working … for …
I wrote two paragraphs: one about then, and one about now.

card.title: Catching up with an old friend
card.situation: You meet your old friend Tomasz in a café. You haven't seen each other for ten years. He asks about your job, your town and your life since you last met.
card.goal: Tell Tomasz how your job or your town has changed, how long you have been doing what you do now, and one thing you have learned.

phrases: It's been ages! How long has it been?
Things have changed a lot since you left.
I left … in … , and I've been working at … since then.
We used to … , but now we … .
prepare.notes: Make notes in three parts: what you did before (the past simple), what has changed (the present perfect), and what you have been doing recently (the present perfect continuous). Add one thing you have learned.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is your old friend. Tell them how your job or your town has changed and what you have learned. Answer their questions, then ask them about their life.
doIt.wehel: You are Tomasz, my old friend. We have not seen each other for ten years, and we meet in a café. Ask me how my job and my town have changed, how long I have been doing my job, and what I have learned. React to my answers and ask follow-up questions. Then tell me a little about your own life. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Two old friends
lines: Ana! I can't believe it. It's been ages!
I know! It's been ten years, hasn't it?
At least. So, are you still at the bank?
No, I left the bank in 2019. I've been working at the council's housing office since then.
Busy! Things have changed a lot since I started. We used to see everyone in person, but now most people apply online.
And the town? It looks so different.
It is. The old bus station has gone, and they've built a shopping centre there.
So what has the new job taught you?
Patience, mostly! And I've learned to use four different computer systems.
I know. I've been taking evening classes for a year, and they've really helped.
compare: Did you use the past simple for a finished time, like I left the bank in 2019?
Did you say how long with since or for?
Did you describe one big change in your job or your town?
Did you say what you have learned?

canDo: I can say how long I have been doing something.
I can choose between the past simple and the present perfect.
I can describe how a job or a town has changed.
I can read an article and a training record, and write about what has changed.
I can tell a friend what has happened and what I have learned.

reading.before: Look at the title and the pictures. What do you think has changed in the story, and over how many years?
reading.talk: What changed in the story, and how did the people adapt? Has something similar happened in your job or your town? Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel about it.

quiz.q: We ___ the new software last week.
quiz.why: Last week is a finished time, so we use the past simple.

quiz.q: He ___ in the same office since 2015.
quiz.why: since + a point in the past, up to now: the present perfect.

quiz.q: How long have you been ___ here?
A move to a more important job in the same company is a ___ .
quiz.why: A promotion gives you a more important job.

quiz.q: This map is ___ . The new road isn't on it.
quiz.why: out of date = old, and not correct any more.

quiz.q: Safety training is ___ : everybody must do it.
quiz.why: compulsory = you must do it, because a rule says so.

quiz.q: We ___ sort the parcels by hand. A machine does it now.
quiz.why: no longer = not now, although it was true before.

quiz.q: When I was a child, we ___ walk to school together every day.
quiz.why: would + verb for an action we did again and again in the past.

quiz.q: I grew ___ in a small village by the sea.
quiz.why: grow up = become an adult in a place.

quiz.q: I ___ have a car, but now I cycle everywhere.
quiz.why: have is a state, so we use used to, not would.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Mei and Omar's conversation in pairs. Then learners interview each other: How long have you been…? What has changed since you started?
Day 2: a timeline on the board. Each learner marks three dates in their working life, and the others ask When did you…? and How long have you been…? Correct the choice of tense.
Day 3: the task. You are the old friend in the café. Each learner tells you how their job or their town has changed and what they have learned.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read their writing about what has changed.
